source.title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Recommendation
source.authors: Wen-Jie Wang; Fu-Li Feng; Xiang-Nan He; Li-Qiang Nie; Tat-Seng Chua

record.tranche_reason: Tests the progression from learning cleaner patterns to fitting noisy interactions in neural recommenders, extending the memorization finding to recommendation data rather than image labels.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on noisy implicit feedback in recommenders. It does not test completely random image labels, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, or the effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation. Results about those other settings are not inferred from its recommender experiments.
record.test_reason: Normal-training loss trajectories test V6 in neural recommendation: clean interactions are fitted earlier, while naturally noisy false-positive interactions are fitted later. This extends the question to implicit feedback rather than randomized classification labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors interpret normal-training trajectories as clean patterns being learned early and noisy interactions eventually being memorized. Their main conclusion is that adaptive truncation or reweighting reduces noisy feedback's influence and improves recommendation quality; the trajectories do not establish zero error on every training interaction.
record.recipe_differences: Studies naturally occurring false-positive implicit interactions in recommenders, comparing training losses over time; it does not randomize image labels or evaluate image-classification test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Training loss method changes the outcome: normal training eventually fits false-positive interactions, T-CE does not optimize over them, and R-CE fits them more slowly. Exact dataset for the Figure 7 comparisons is not stated in the result text.

fits_no_version.finding: T-CE increases false-positive CE loss while overall training loss decreases; R-CE slows false-positive fitting and retains a loss gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Discarding or down-weighting large-loss interactions can reduce fitting of naturally noisy implicit feedback.

record.problems: Relevant loss trajectories are presented in figures without exact numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The Figure 7 result text does not state the dataset. The experiments concern naturally occurring noisy recommendation feedback, not random image labels.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results were found. Figure 9 reports how Truncated Loss identifies false-positive interactions, but that is a denoising-method diagnostic rather than a result measuring the behavior named in V6.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A controlled label-corruption sweep, perfect training fit throughout, and steady test-error degradation toward chance.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.

Completely random labels and direct identification of shared patterns versus example-specific memorization; the experiments use naturally occurring false-positive feedback identified through dwell time or ratings.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Naturally noisy feedback falls within V6's noisy-label component. The deliberately modified ADT objectives do not warrant the record's limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels on training images, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training time for random versus true labels and convergence as the fraction of corrupted labels changes.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
A sweep from no corrupted labels to all labels corrupted, perfect training fit across that sweep, and test-error progression toward chance.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on fitting random labels and generalization on true labels.
Tests naturally occurring false-positive implicit feedback in recommenders, not completely random labels or image classifiers; does not test the Arpit et al. image-classification setup.

rows.subject: NeuMF
rows.operation_detail: Compared training loss for true-positive and false-positive interactions over normal training.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss of true-positive and false-positive interactions
rows.baseline: True-positive interaction loss, as the reference
rows.value: Figure only; text says false-positive loss is clearly larger early and both losses converge to close values eventually.
rows.note: Text states the qualitative pattern; no exact plotted values are reported.
rows.check: No substantive correction. NeuMF on Adressa has higher false-positive than true-positive loss early, followed by convergence to similar losses. This measures relative learning dynamics, not zero classification error.

rows.subject: GMF
rows.operation_detail: Measured false-positive interaction loss during normal training, against real training loss.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss of false-positive interactions over training
rows.baseline: All training interactions' loss, shown as the reference
rows.value: Figure only; text says false-positive interaction loss eventually becomes similar to other interactions.
rows.note: The text explicitly says GMF fits false-positive interactions well at last; dataset is not identified in the supplied result text.
rows.check: The reference is all training interactions, not clean interactions alone. Figure 7(a) and Section 5.2.1 report eventual fitting of false-positive interactions; the dataset is unspecified. This complements R1 but provides a less direct clean-versus-noisy comparison.

rows.subject: GMF+T-CE
rows.operation_detail: Applied Truncated Cross-Entropy loss during training.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss of false-positive interactions and overall training loss over training
rows.baseline: Normal training is shown in Figure 7(a); exact baseline value not stated
rows.value: Figure only; text says false-positive loss increases while overall training loss decreases stably.
rows.note: The paper says the increased loss indicates parameters are not optimized over false-positive interactions.
rows.check: Exclude from claim verdicts: this is a diagnostic of the authors' mitigation method. T-CE deliberately discards large-loss interactions; increasing false-positive loss does not establish a failure of V6's ordinary learning dynamics.

rows.subject: GMF+R-CE
rows.operation_detail: Applied Reweighted Cross-Entropy loss during training.
rows.measure: Cross-entropy loss of false-positive interactions over training
rows.baseline: Real training loss, shown as the reference
rows.value: Figure only; text says false-positive loss decreases but remains larger than real training loss.
rows.note: The paper says R-CE still fits false-positive interactions, though more slowly and with smaller weights.
rows.check: Exclude from claim verdicts: R-CE deliberately down-weights hard interactions. Its altered loss trajectory measures mitigation performance, not an independent scope limit on V6. The reference is all training interactions.

relationships.condition: Normal training of NeuMF on Adressa and GMF in the unspecified Figure 7 setting
relationships.reason: R1 shows lower clean-interaction loss early and similar clean/noisy losses eventually; R2 corroborates eventual fitting of false-positive interactions under normal training.
relationships.display_finding: Clean interactions had lower losses early, but clean and noisy losses eventually converged as false-positive interactions were fitted.
